analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.
analysis.headline: The estate tax repeal bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on its first day and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the federal estate tax, the gift tax, and the generation-skipping transfer tax — the taxes that apply when large amounts of wealth are handed from one person to another, often across generations. Only the largest estates ever owe the estate tax; in 2013 the tax only reached estates above roughly $5 million per couple (that threshold is general knowledge about how the tax works, not from these sources). The bill was referred to the tax-writing committee the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs and families of the very largest estates, since the tax applies only to estates above several million dollars. Wealthy families with large planned inheritances would keep that wealth entirely free of federal transfer tax.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals all of Subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, eliminating the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes outright, effective for deaths and transfers after enactment.
The repeal would apply to the estates of people dying and gifts made after the date of enactment.
Because the estate tax exempts a large exclusion amount before applying, the direct benefit of repeal flows to estates in the millions of dollars and up.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately general taxpayers, since estate and gift tax revenue would be eliminated entirely. Revenue from these taxes funds general government spending, so repealing them would either mean higher deficits or higher taxes and lower spending elsewhere.
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers and the federal Treasury

drawbacks.text: Repeal eliminates an entire revenue stream from the tax code; the Joint Committee on Taxation had historically scored full estate tax repeal at well over $200 billion in lost revenue per decade (this figure is general knowledge about fiscal scoring, not from these sources).

The tax structure the bill repeals applies only to the largest transfers — Subtitle B covers estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes — so repeal is a tax cut whose direct beneficiaries are families holding very large wealth, while its costs are spread across all federal taxpayers.

Estate tax repeal also removes the step that keeps accumulated unrealized gains from passing entirely untaxed between generations; under current law the estate tax is the main backstop taxing large unrealized gains at death (mechanism is general knowledge about the tax system).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits go to a narrow group — heirs of estates large enough to owe the tax — while its cost, the loss of all estate and gift tax revenue, is spread across every federal taxpayer through higher deficits or higher other taxes. There is no provision in the bill to offset the lost revenue.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on January 3, 2013, the first day of the 113th Congress.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote — through the end of the Congress.
The bill had 53 cosponsors: 51 Republicans and 2 Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers overall are better off that it died, since the bill offered no offset for the revenue it would have removed from the largest estates. Wealthy families never got the repeal, so no one gained the tax savings the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; the repeal never happened

for.name: Rep. Mac Thornberry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 113th Congress and lined up 53 cosponsors.

for.name: 51 of 232 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the estate tax repeal bill.

for.name: 2 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making its sponsorship nearly but not entirely along party lines.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after the bill's referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving it to expire.

against.name: Speaker John Boehner and House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote during the two-year Congress, despite the majority party's own members supplying nearly all its cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was heavily partisan — 51 of 53 cosponsors were Republicans — though two House Democrats also signed on.

industries.industry: Heirs of very large estates and family wealth
industries.note: Repeal would let the largest estates pass entirely free of federal transfer tax, with the revenue loss spread across all taxpayers. The estate tax's large exemption means the benefit is concentrated at the top of the wealth distribution.

industries.industry: Estate planning attorneys and wealth advisors
industries.note: Repeal would eliminate the compliance work around estate and gift filings, though these firms also earn fees helping families navigate the current tax. The effect on ordinary people is negligible.
